Polyphase magnetization of the Big Spruce Complex, Northwest Territories1 
E. IRVING AND J. C. MCGLYNN 
Departtnent of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa, Canada. 
The Big Spruce alkaline complex has yielded a Rb-Sr isochron of 21 11 + 40 m. y. The rocks are 
unmetamorphosed, but the local geochrono1ogical evidence indicates that they have had a 
complicated thermal history. The complex has four magnetizations, which can be separated by a 
two-stage demagnetization procedure. The D magnetization (19 sites; 022, +88; %, =So; pole 67" 
N 113" W) is considered to have been acquired at the time of emplacement because it generally has 
the highest blocking temperatures (500 to 650 "C). The X, Y, and Z magnetizations are believed to 
be later overprints, as they generally have lower blocking temperatures and have directions that 
are comparable to those found in younger rocks in the interval of approximately 2000 to 1400 m.y. 
Most of the overprints seem to have been acquired at times of mild reheatingduring this interval.

[Traduit par le journal] 
Can. J. Earth Sci.. 13.476489(1976) 
Introduction 
Polyphase magnetization is the phenomenon 
whereby a rock unit may contain several different 
magnetizations, each corresponding to the geo- 
magnetic field at various times during the history 
of the rock unit. These magnetizations may be 
present in different oxide phases, or in different 
grain-size ranges of the same oxide phase. They 
can be separated by chemical leaching, which 
progressively removes the finer grain-size frac- 
tions and the magnetizations they carry; by al- 
ternating field (AF) demagnetization, which pro- 
gressively removes the magnetizations of lower 
remanent coercive force; or by thermal demag- 
netization, which progressively removes the 
magnetizations with lower blocking tempera- 
tures. The phenomenon of polyphase magnetiza- 
tion is analogous to polyphase deformation in 
metamorphic rocks, which is indicative of a 
complex metamorphic history, and to the occur- 
rence of a spread of apparent dates obtained in 
geochronological studies, which is indicative 
of a complex thermal history. 
One of the simplest situations in paleomag- 
netism is that in which there is a primary mag- 
'Earth Physics Branch Contribution No. 588. 
netization, on which a second magnetization due 
to the present field is imposed. Such secondary 
magnetizations can be readily removed by partial 
AF or thermal demagnetization. The next most 
complex case is that in which magnetizations 
have been acauired at some more remote time, 
usually during deep burial and uplift; permiad 
overprints in Devonian and Silurian red beds 
(Chamalaun 1964; Irving and Opdyke 1965), 
and old overprints in Precambrian rocks 
(McMurry et al. 1973; Buchan and Dunlop 
1973; Irving et al. 1974) have been documented. 
However, the magnetization of rocks that have 
been subjected to a series of episodes of reheating 
or chemical change over an interval during which 
the field has greatly changed, is much more com- 
plex. The primary magnetization may have been 
partially or completely replaced by two or more 
secondary magnetizations, and the identification 
of these magnetizations, and the determination 
of their order in time, are the most important 
technical problems in Precambrian paleomag- 
netism. Recently, Roy and Park (1974) have 
shown that certain Carboniferous red beds de- 
posited during an interval when the geomagnetic 
field was reversing frequently contained three 
magnetizations (two reversed and one normal),

and Park (1975) has recognized four magnetiza- 
tions in the metamorphic rocks near Flin Flon. 
In this paper we describe an instance ofpolyphase 
magnetization in unmetamorphosed igneous 
rocks. 
Geology 
The Big Spruce Complex occurs about 140 km 
northwest of Yellowknife (Fig. 1). It intrudes 
Archean granitic and supracrustal rocks of the 
Slave Structural Province. Martineau and Lam- 
bert (1974) have shown that the northeastern part 
consists of silica-saturated layered diorites and 
gabbros intruded by magnetite-rich pyroxenites 
and a syenite ring dike (Fig. 2). The rest of the 
complex comprises silica-saturated and over- 
saturated syenites, and undersaturated foyaites 
and ijolites, which we refer to collectively as 
'syenites'. There are local swarms of thin basic 
dikes and a carbonatite plug. Fenites are well 
developed about the margins of the silica-under- 
saturated rocks, and gas explosion vents with 
related breccias also occur near contacts. The 
intrusion is cut by a small fault, and there is some 
indication from the regional geology that it lies 
in a major fault zone. The rocks commonly show 
internal fracturing, but there is no evidence of 
thermal metamorphism. 
Martineau and Lambert (1974) obtained an 
Rb-Sr whole-rock isochron from the complex 
yielding an age of 2111 + 40 m.y. (A = 1.39 x 
10- l1 years). They also obtained an isochron of 
1925 f 40 m.y. from a nearby small biotite 
pyroxenite complex. Martineau and Lambert 
reported K-Ar mineral ages of 1800 m.y., and a 
biotite collected by W. R. A. Baragar yielded a

been raised so the Complex is now almost entirely under

K-Ar age of 1785 m.y. (Leech et al. 1963). The 
granites into which the complex is intruded 
yielded Rb-Sr isochron ages in the range of 
2400-2600 m.y. In this paper, we have accepted 
2111 f 40 m.y. as the age of intrusion of the 
complex. 
Procedures 
Oriented cores (1 1 l altogether) were collected 
from 22 sites and their distribution is shown on 
Fig. 2. About five cores were collected at each 
site, and two samples were sliced from each core. 
Orientations were measured by sun compass. 
Contact samples of Yellowknife Supergroup 
sedimentary rocks were collected at site A1 12 
(the directions were close to the present field and 
became scattered in alternating fields of 100 Oe 
and yielded no useful information). Contact 
rocks were sought elsewhere, but not found. 
Magnetizations were measured using a Princeton 
Applied Research Spinner magnetometer (SMI) 
SCI. VOL. 13, 1976 
and Schonstedt spinner magnetometers (SSMI 
and DSM1). Alternating field (AF peak ampli- 
tudes quoted) and thermal demagnetization was 
carried out using the apparatus described by Roy 
et al. (1969; 1971 ; 1973). A three-axis tumbler 
was used during AF .demagnetization. Both 
thermal and AF demagnetization were carried 
out in fields of less than 2 gammas. 
All specimens contain a large, magnetically 
soft component, which can be readily removed 
by alternating fields of about 100 Oe, and which 
commonly reduces the remanence to between 
10% and 1% of its original value. The magnetiza- 
tion remaining is itself composite, but it cannot 
be resolved into its constituent magnetizations 
by further AF demagnetization. The technique 
that we have found most useful in analyzing 
these polyphase magnetizations is a two-stage 
demagnetization procedure (Park 1975). The 
large soft magnetizations were first removed by 
AF demagnetization, and then thermal demag- 
netization was used. Presumably, the reason 
why this two-stage demagnetization technique 
is successful while the application of AF demag- 
netization alone is not is that, in general, the 
remanent coercive force spectra of the constitu- 
ent magnetizations overlap, but their blocking 
temperature spectra do not. The magnetization 
remaining after initial AF demagnetization is 
less than lo%, and sometimes less than I%, of 
the original magnetization. Furthermore, its 
constituent magnetizations may comprise only 
a few parts of one per cent of the original mag- 
netization, so that the acquisition of spurious 
magnetizations during demagnetization, due say 
to departures from perfect field cancellation, 
could lead to serious distortion of the results. 
Great care has been exercised to ensure that 
spurious magnetizations have been minimized 
and are random in direction. In any one thermal 
demagnetization run, the specimens are stored 
randomly in the furnace; they have been demag- 
netized in many different batches over a period of 
three years, using three different magnetometers. 
Between demagnetization and measurement, 
specimens have been stored in random orienta- 
tions in mumetal shields, inside which the field 
is less than 5 gammas. 
Resolution of X, Y, Z and D Magnetizations 
The basic rocks from the north of the complex 
are very magnetic (Table 1). Their remanent 
magnetizations are complex and results from

Pyroxenite from Site CIll 
The results of AF demagnetization of a speci- 
men from pyroxenite at site Clll are shown in 
Fig. 3. Its direction is little changed in fields up 
to 600 Oe, and in higher fields the directions 
scatter. The intensity falls very rapidly, being less 
than 0.2% of the original value (the natural 
remanent magnetization nrm) in fields above 400 
Oe. Over 99.8% of the nrm consists of a relatively 
soft magnetization that is directed to the SSW 
with low positive inclination. Magnetizations 
with this general direction are referred to as X 
magnetization. The X magnetization diverges 
from the present field by a large angle and there- 
fore cannot be a viscous magnetization of recent 
origin.

from site CI 11. The intensity is plotted on a log scale. The 
corresponding direction changes are shown as dots repre-

In Fig. 4, the resolution of the magnetization 
remaining after AF demagnetization in 400 Oe 
is shown. The average directions of all specimens 
from site C111 are shown. Thermal demagnetiza- 
tion up to 300 "C does not change the direction, 
but at 400 "C the inclinations increase abruptly 
and then remain essentially constant up to 
650 "C. Magnetizations with steeply inclined 
downward directions are referred to as the D 
magnetizations. The corresponding intensity 
changes are given in the lower part of Fig. 4. 
The intensity falls by a factor of 3, and is less 
than 0.1% of the nrm after thermal demagnetiza- 
tion between 500 and 650 "C. Thus, that part 
of the X magnetization with remanent coerciv- 
ities exceeding 400 Oe has blocking temperatures 
of less than 400 "C. Most of the D magnetization 
has blocking temperatures in excess of 650°C. 
There may be some blocking temperatures in the 
range 500 to 650°C, but the noise inherent in 
this extreme demagnetization process (as shown 
by the standard errors in the decay curves) do 
not allow this to be definitely determined. The 
directions of the D and X magnetizations at C111 
are listed in Table 1. The D magnetization is the

The main opaque phases are ilmenite com- 
monly rimmed with leucoxene, and magnetite 
with fine and coarse ilmenite lamellae. The mag- 
netite-ilmenite grains are large (100 to 1000 pm), 
but because of intergrowths the effective grain 
size of the magnetite is probably much less. The 
large X magnetization presumably resides in this 
magnetite. Minor opaque phases are hematite, 
pyrite partly altered to geothite, and pyrrhotite 
partly altered to marcasite. The hematite occurs 
dispersed in silicate minerals as very fine needles 
(1-5 pm) commonly oriented parallel to the 
cleavage, and it is considered to be the source 
of the D magnetization.

and 600 Oe, and the scattered directions and variable 
intensities produced in higher fields. This apparent end- 
point is not a single magnetization but a combination of 
Y and D magnetizations that can be resolved by thermal 
demagnetization (Fig. 6). The initial (nrm) intensity is

irregular way around the apparent end-point 
direction, but at 600 "C the inclination increases, 
and the direction moves into the field of the D 
magnetization and remains there until 650 "C. 
Thus the apparent end-point magnetization 
actually consists of two magnetizations: a D 
magnetization and a magnetization obtained by 
subtracting vectorially the D magnetization from 
the apparent end-point magnetization. This has 
a NW declination with negative inclination. It is 
labelled AF (C) in Fig. 6 and is referred to as the 
Y magnetization. The separation of the D and Y 
magnetizations in a single specimen is shown in 
Table 2. Thus, the nrm consists of three com- 
ponents, D and Y together with an X magnetiza- 
tion (marked NRM (C) in Fig. 6), which is ob- 
tained by subtracting D and Y from the nrm. 
The mean directions of these three magnetiza- 
tions are listed in Table 1. The corresponding 
intensity variations are shown in the lower part 
of Fig. 6. They are irregular, but there is a drop 
in intensity between 550 and 600 "C that corre- 
sponds to the rotation of the direction into the 
D field. Apparently the blocking temperature of 
the Y magnetization is predominantly between 
550 and 600 "C, whereas the blocking tempera- 
ture of the D magnetization is between 600 and 
650 "C or above. This suggests that Y and D are 
carried by magnetite and hematite, respectively. 
The oxide phases are similar to those at site 
Cl 11 except that the ilmenite is fresh, leucoxene 
rare, and sulphides are unaltered. The X and Y 
magnetizations presumably reside in the mag- 
netite of the magnetite-ilmenite grains, the 
former in the larger grains. The hematite needles 
in the silicates are the probable carriers of the D 
magnetization.

The oxide phases are similar to those observed 
at site Clll except that the ilmenite is fresh 
and leucoxene rare. The magnetite-ilmenite 
grains contain small blebs of a mineral that could 
not be firmly identified, but which may be hema- 
tite. As before, hematite occurs as fine needles 
in the silicates, and in addition, larger blebs of 
magnetite and hematite also occur in the silicates. 
Hematite is presumably the carrier of the D 
magnetization. The Z magnetization presum- 
ably is carried by magnetite. 
Syenite 
The magnetization of the syenites is much 
simpler. D magnetizations predominate. Y mag- 
netizations only are found at two sites (A115, 
B20). The AF demagnetization curves again fall 
rapidly (Fig. 9), and usually move into the D 
field after demagnetization in fields between 100 
and 300 Oe. Thermal demagnetization after AF 
cleaning (the intensity is then usually between 5 
and 10x of nrm) yields the mean curve of Fig. 
10 with blocking temperatures between 500 and 
600 "C, indicating that magnetite is responsible 
for the D magnetization. 
The dominant opaque mineral is ilmenite, 
occasionally extensively altered to leucoxene. 
Magnetite occurs as small discrete grains asso-

ciated with ilmenite and as inclusions in ilmenite. 
Although magnetite is apparently responsible for 
remanence, it is not seen in many sections, but 
only very small quantities are required to pro- 
duce the observed remanence. Amorphous hema- 
tite occurs as fine dust in some of the silicates. 
Analysis of Directions 
Of the 22 sites sampled, all but two gave co- 
herent data. At sites A1 14 and (2112, scattered 
directions were observed and no coherent mag- 
netization could be found. The magnetizations 
at each collecting site are listed in Table 1 and 
plotted in Fig. 11. The mean directions of the 
four magnetizations are given in Table 3. All 
syenite sites except B20 and A1 15 yielded D 
magnetizations. B20 and A1 15 have Y magneti- 
zations only. Most sites in basic rocks from the 
northern part of the complex yielded several 
magnetizations, and the D magnetization is 
present at all except site C118. The X, Y, and Z 
magnetizations are distributed in an irregular 
way, and there is no systematic relationship to 
rock types. The D magnetization is present at 
most sites (19 out of 20). The Y magnetization 
contains reversals. The separation of the X, Y, 
and Z magnetizations is arbitrary, and although 
there do seem to be three distinct groups, it could

In Figs. 12 and 13, the poles corresponding to 
the magnetizations observed in the Big Spruce 
Complex are plotted and compared with paths 
of apparent polar wander (APW) constructed 
previously. In Fig. 12, the pole corresponding to 
the D magnetization and other poles for the 
interval 2200 to 1800 m.y. are shown. They form 
a reasonably coherent array, stretching from 
what is nowadays the Mackenzie delta to Peru. 
This APW path is referred to as track 5. Readers 
are referred to papers by McGlynn et al. (1975) 
and Irving and McGlynn (1976) for a discussion 
of track 5 and its tectonic significance. One 
notable feature is the excellent agreement be- 
tween the poles for the Otto Stock and the D 
magnetization of the Big Spruce Complex. These 
bodies have statistically similar Rb-Sr ages 
(see caption to Fig. 12). Studies of the metamor- 
phic aureole of the Otto Stock have shown that 
the remanence was acquired during cooling 
following instrusion (Pullaiah and Irving 1975). 
Moreover, the D magnetization has directions 
that are different from those in any neighbouring 
rock unit. Hence, it is reasonable to suppose that 
the D magnetization of the Big Spruce Complex 
was acquired at the time of initial cooling, be- 
tween 2150 and 2070 m.y. 
The mean direction of the D magnetization 
is not significantly different from the present 
field (Fig. 1 1 and Table 3) and it might be argued, 
therefore, that it is a very tenacious viscous or 
weathering magnetization of recent origin, 
aligned along the present field. It seems to us that 
this is very unlikely, because the blocking tem- 
peratures are very high; because the carrier of 
the D magnetization in the syenites is magnetite, 
not hematite (Fig. 10); because the rocks are 
fresh, being taken from cores drilled from be- 
neath the outer crust; and because there is no 
evidence of weathering of magnetite or hematite 
in polished and thin sections. The crystalline 
hematite in the silicates of the basic rocks is ap- 
parently a product of primary crystallization. 
In Fig. 13, a reconstruction of the APW path 
for the interval 1800 to 1300 m.y. is shown. This 
is referred to as track 4. References may be made 
to Park et al. (1973), McGlynn et al. (1974), and 
Irving and McGlynn (1976) for discussions of 
track 4. Tracks 4 and 5 cross one another in

what is now Central America. Using this track 
as a scale for determining the age ofmagnetiza- 
tion, then the Z magnetizations (poles near 
eastern South America) appear to be about 1800 
m.y. old, and the X magnetizations (poles in the 
central Pacific) appear to be about 1400 m.y. 
old. The poles for the Y magnetizations (poles 
near Central America), however, fall 'on the 
cross-over of tracks 4 and 5, and hence may be 
assigned an age of either about 1900 or about 
1600 m.y. It is noteworthy that the Y magnetiza- 
tions are similar in direction to those observed 
from the Indin Dikes (2093 f 86 m.y., Gates 
and Hurley 1973), which approach to within 
20 km of the Big Spruce Complex (Fig. 1). Also, 
Martineau and Lambert (1974) have obtained 
and Rb-Sr whole-rock isochron of 1926 f 40 
m.y. from a nearby biotite pyroxenite complex. 
Thus there is evidence of thermal events near 
the Big Spruce Complex between 2100 and 1900 
m.y. BP, and the Y magnetizations could have 
been acquired during that interval. The Z mag- 
netization may correspond in time to the K-Ar 
biotite age of 1785 m.y. from the Big Spruce 
Complex (Leech et al. 1963), which presumably 
reflects post-Hudsonian uplift. Thus, the Y and 
Z magnetizations may be associated with identi- 
fiable local thermal events at about 2000 and 
1800 m.y. BP, respectively. There is no known 
local thermal event about 1400 m.y. ago with 
which the X magnetization could be identified. 
Origin of Polyphase Magnetization 
In the previous section approximate ages 
spanning about 800 m.y. have been assigned to 
the four magnetizations. A number of blocking 
temperatureranges are present, which indicates 
that the magnetizations are carried by different 
iron oxide phases. Observation of polished sec- 
tions shows that several oxide phases are indeed 
present. The polyphase magnetization therefore 
could have originated either by changes in the 
composition or grain-size relationships of the 
iron oxides, or by thermal processes operating 
over this 800 m.y. interval. The geochronological 
evidence indicates a complex thermal history. 
There could have been a single episode of very 
slow cooling, or a number of heating and cooling 
episodes. Thermal and chemical processes may 
have operated together. The magnetite observed 
in polished sections is fresh, and the hematite 
grains within the silicates are also fresh, and there 
is no reason to believe that they are not the prod- 
uct of initial crystallization. Alteration of il- 
menite to leucoxene and sulphides to goethite 
occur at 5 sites (B20, B22, B24, B29, Cl1 l), but

temperatures of the Y magnetization are mainly 
between 500 and 600 "C, at one site (C118) be-

tures of the Z magnetization are in the range 500 
to 600 "C. The blocking temperatures of the X 
magnetization are between 200 to 400 "C. The 
highest blocking temperatures (above 600 "C) 
occur in the D magnetization associated with 
hematite in the basic phases of the northern part 
of the intrusion. In the Z and X magnetizations, 
such high blocking temperatures are not found, 
and crystalline hematite is not observed. In the 
Y magnetization, blocking temperatures as high 
as 600 "C occur only at one site. Thus, there is a

500 to 650 "C, the range in about one half of the sing pole at 67" N 11 lo W agrees very well with

### page_13
488 CAN. J. EARTH SCI. VOL. 13, 1976 
the poles from the Otto Stock and the Big Spruce 
Complex, and the three bodies are, within the 
errors, of the same age. Symons and Londry, how- 
ever, reject the pole at 67" N 11 1" W as being due 
to magnetization by the present field; but the 
magnetizations are just a; stable as other mag- 
netizations from the Nipissing diabase (Symons 
and Londry 1975, their fig. 4), and Pullaiah and 
Irving (1975) have shown that similarly directed 
magnetizations in the Otto Stock are not caused 
by the present earth's field, but were acquired dur- 
ingcoolingafter emplacement. Hence it is possible, 
as Irving and McGlynn (1976) have contended, 
that the second Nipissing pole at 14" S 100" W 
is an overprint. On this view the Otto, Big 
Spruce, and Nipissing bodies have the same 
paleomagnetic pole near the present western 
Arctic coast of Canada, and they are part of a 
major rifting event at about 2100 m.y. that fol- 
lowed the deposition of Huronian sedimentary 
rocks.
